item.title: Mondriaan painting set to fetch €30m at auction later this year
item.description:
Mondriaan painting set to fetch €30m at auction later this year

August 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A painting by the Dutch artist Piet Mondriaan is expected to sell for more than €30 million when it goes under the hammer later this year.

The work, Composition III, dates from 1920, the year Mondriaan returned to Paris to develop his distinctive abstract style of Neo-Plasticism.

The painting, which has been in a private collection for the last 25 years, is expected to fetch the highest price this autumn when London auction house Christie’s puts it up for sale on October 14.

“It is a very rare work from the year that you really see Mondriaan finding his feet and developing his neoplastic theory as an artist,” Keith Gill, head of impressionist and modern art at Christie’s said.

Mondriaan finished just eight paintings in 1920, five of which are owned by major museums such as the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, the Tate in London and the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Christie’s estimates it will sell for between £20 mln and £20 mln (€23 mln-€35 mln), but Gill said that could prove to be a conservative estimate.

“Given the importance of this masterpiece and the outstanding condition it is in, it could easily fetch more,” he told the Telegraaf.

The record price for a Mondriaan was set in November 1922, when Composition no. II sold for $51 million (€49.4 mln) at Sotheby’s in New York.

item.title: New in NL: Should you go for a traditional Dutch bank or go neo?
item.description:
Partner content

New in NL: Should you go for a traditional Dutch bank or go neo?

August 26, 2026

The financial services industry in the Netherlands has changed enormously in recent years, shaken up by the internet, changing customer demand and banking apps. So what is best for you – an account with a more traditional bank or an online-only version?

One of the first things you need to do when establishing yourself in the Netherlands is to set up a bank account, so you are ready to pay rent, use public transport and access your salary as soon as you hit the ground.

The rise of fintech – technology-driven financial services – and neo banks, which are online-only alternatives to traditional banks, has increased the choices available to expats, but there are some things to consider before you decide what sort of bank to go for.

Ask questions in English

For a start, think about how you want to communicate with your bank. Are you happy using a chatbot to get answers to your questions – or, as often happens, one that fails to give you a proper answer at all? Or would you prefer to speak directly to a human being?

ABN Amro, for example, has a team of English-language advisors who are there to answer your questions by phone or online. You can set up a face-to-face online meeting with one of them from anywhere in the world, before you have even arrived.

Decades of experience

Another important difference between more traditional banks and the fintechs comes down to experience. Traditional banks have many more years of experience in helping clients and know what makes them tick. ABN Amro has been serving hundreds of thousands of internationals and expats for over 25 years, devising products which are directly tailored to their needs.

In addition, the traditional Dutch banks are all rooted in the Netherlands, so they are well versed in their domestic market and understand local financial needs.

Expat banking can be complicated

Unlike neo banks, traditional banks also operate high-street branches where you can go personally to sort out paperwork or other issues which are difficult to deal with online. Expats, in particular, may have more complicated financial needs, such as being paid a salary in a different currency.

In addition, neo banks and fintechs mainly offer current and savings accounts but not the other financial services which you need to establish yourself in the Netherlands, which means you cannot take care of all your financial needs under one roof.

That’s fine, of course, if you are happy shopping around. But if simplicity and ease are important to you, it would be sensible to look at a bank which offers wider services.

Think insurance, for example, or pensions, or a mortgage – if you are planning to stay in the Netherlands for longer. Traditional banks cater to your long-term financial needs, not just your immediate ones, offering more specialist wealth management and private banking services as well as instant payments and cash withdrawals.

Online banking services

Of course, traditional banks have evolved alongside digital-first providers, offering many of the same online banking features that customers expect today. You can bank via your phone, use your (online) direct debit card at home and abroad, seamlessly make and accept payments in other currencies and keep a close eye on your daily spending patterns – all of which are part of the modern approach to banking.

In that sense, the difference between a high-street and an online bank is virtually non-existent. The main differences become apparent when customers need personal support or access to a broader range of financial services which the neo banks don’t offer.

In fact, there may even be financial advantages to opening an account with a more traditional bank! ABN Amro, for example, is currently offering up to €175 cashback for new customers who open their first current account.

item.title: Feyenoord fans face ban from Nijmegen for setting off fireworks
item.description:
Feyenoord fans face ban from Nijmegen for setting off fireworks

August 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The mayor of Nijmegen, Hubert Bruls, has threatened to ban Feyenoord fans from the Goffertstadion next month unless those responsible for letting off fireworks during last weekend’s match at Cambuur Leeuwarden are arrested.

Seven home fans were injured when a barrage of fireworks went off in the away supporters’ enclosure in the twelfth minute of Sunday’s match in De Kooi stadium.

Police are investigating how the banned explosives got into the stadium, but have so far made no arrests. The fans who set off the flares had their faces covered.

“We need to take a stand together,” Bruls told talk show Goedenavond Nederland. “The first thing we need to do is catch the culprits. But if that fails, I’m prepared to say that away supporters won’t be welcome next time or in future.”

Feyenoord won the match 5-2 after a 20-minute break. Referee Danny Makkelie later questioned guidelines that say a match should be abandoned if a player is struck by objects thrown from the crowd, but nothing about injuries to supporters.

“It’s an agreement made between the clubs, not us,” Makkelie explained. “I don’t know what the reason for it is, because it’s just as bad whether players or supporters are hit.”

item.title: Israel expels two Dutch officials over settlement goods ban
item.description:
Israel expels two Dutch officials over settlement goods ban

August 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Israel is expelling two Dutch officials from the US-backed centre that coordinates the Gaza ceasefire, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements.

Israeli foreign minister Gideon Saar said on social media on Tuesday that the pair would be removed from the coordination centre in the southern city of Kiryat Gat and had one week to leave the country. The decision was taken with the approval of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Saar cited “a series of anti-Israel measures” by the Dutch government, the most recent being its ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, which takes effect on September 22.

The two are a member of staff at the Dutch embassy in Israel and an official from the Netherlands’ representation in Ramallah, both serving as observers at the centre, news agency ANP reported.

“Our message is clear: those who act against Israel will have no foothold in the region,” Saar said. He also claimed the Dutch government’s policy had been accompanied by “an unprecedented wave of antisemitism and boycotts” in the Netherlands.

Gaza aid centre
The centre was set up as the Civil-Military Coordination Center under US president Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza, bringing together representatives from more than a dozen countries – including the Netherlands – to monitor the ceasefire, oversee aid and help plan the territory’s reconstruction.

The Netherlands is the second country to be expelled from the centre, after Israel removed Spain in April. The move is the latest in a series of diplomatic clashes: Israel summoned the Dutch ambassador last year over travel bans imposed on two far-right Israeli ministers.

Dutch response
Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said he regretted the expulsion, calling it “an unnecessary action” that he had raised immediately with Saar. He linked the move to the Israeli elections at the end of October.

Berendsen said the settlement-goods ban would not change and that aid to Gaza was still badly needed to carry out the commitments made under Trump’s plan. He said he respected Israel’s decision but remained willing to discuss it.

The Dutch cabinet agreed the three-year ban in May. It bars the import, sale and trade of goods from illegal settlements in territories occupied by Israel.

Last week the Netherlands joined six other governments in condemning Israel’s decision to open bidding on a major West Bank settlement project.

item.title: NEC out of Champions League after early red card kills hopes
item.description:
NEC out of Champions League after early red card kills hopes

August 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

NEC Nijmegen will play in the Europa League group phase after going down to a comprehensive 6-1 aggregate defeat on Tuesday night to Bodø/Glimt in their Champions League play-off.

Clement Bischoff’s late goal in the first leg had given Dick Schreuder’s side a glimmer of hope, but it was extinguished in the second minute when goalkeeper Gonzalo Crettaz was sent off for handling outside the penalty area.

The 10 men held out until just before half-time, when former Feyenoord defender Fredrik Bjørkan and Sondre Auklend took advantage of the gaping holes in NEC’s defence to score twice in three minutes.

NEC suffered further pain when Deveron Fonville deflected a cross into his own net, while Auklend shot wide of an open goal in the closing minutes.

Schreuder admitted his plans to overturn the 3-1 deficit from the first leg had gone up in smoke when Crettaz blocked a through ball with his hand.

“You can come up with all sorts of things, but several things we could have done better went wrong in that one moment,” he told Ziggo Sport.

“When I look at how they fought and how the boys who came in played, I’m incredibly proud. I can’t fault them.”

NEC will learn their opponents in the Europa League group stage when the draw takes place on Friday.

item.title: Students who leave home rarely move far, CBS finds
item.description:
Students who leave home rarely move far, CBS finds

August 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Most young people in the Netherlands who leave home to study move to a university city in their own region, figures from the national statistics office CBS show.

Nearly 32,000 people aged 17 to 22 moved out to live in a university city in 2025. More than 80% came from a different municipality, but most had not gone far.

Amsterdam and Groningen took in the most, with 5,300 and 5,100 – the only cities to draw more than 5,000. About 30% of those who moved to Amsterdam or Rotterdam had already been living there, and many of the rest came from within 50 kilometres.

Groningen draws students mainly from the three northern provinces, Enschede from the east, and Maastricht, Tilburg and Eindhoven from Noord-Brabant and Limburg. Wageningen is the exception, taking students from across the country.
The figures count only domestic moves and leave out international students.

Around 17% of university students in the Netherlands come from abroad, a share that climbs above 60% in Maastricht.

Fewer young people are leaving home to study than a decade ago, down from an average of 36,000 a year between 2015 and 2021, as more stay put. The number spiked above 50,000 in 2023, the year the basic student grant returned and made moving out more affordable.

Where they go also splits along gender lines. Over the five years to 2025, women made up about two-thirds of new arrivals in Maastricht and Nijmegen, while the three cities with a technical university – Delft, Eindhoven and Enschede – drew more men.

item.title: New Oranje coach Xavi calls Netherlands “university of football”
item.description:
New Oranje coach Xavi calls Netherlands “university of football”

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New national head coach Xavi Hernandez said he regarded the Netherlands as the “university of football” as he gave his first press conference in Zeist.

The 46-year-old said it was an “honour” to be appointed by the KNVB as the first foreign coach since Austria’s Ernst Happel led the men’s team to the 1978 World Cup final.

Xavi was the KNVB’s third choice for the job after Pep Guardiola, the former Manchester City coach, opted to take a sabbatical from football and Arne Slot, the former Feyenoord and Liverpool coach, preferred to stay in club football.

He has been given a four-year contract until the end of the next World Cup in 2030, with no conditions tied to the Netherlands’ performance at the European Championships in two years’ time.

Most of Xavi’s playing career was spent at Barcelona, where he won eight La Liga titles, many of them under the tutelage of Guardiola, whose playing style was influenced by Dutch legend Johan Cruyff.

He made his international debut for Spain in a friendly game against the Netherlands in 2000 and 10 years later was one of the pivotal members of the team that won the World Cup in 2010, defeating Oranje in the final.

“My feeling today is that I’m going to the university of football,” Xavi said. “I learned a lot during my career as a player and a coach that I want to give back.

Big family

“I believe a lot in this generation,” he added. “We have a lot of talents, but the important thing for me is to create a team, a group and a big family in order to play well.”

Asked how he felt about being the KNVB’s third choice, ahead of youth team coach Michael Reiziger, Xavi said: “It’s not a bad position after Guardiola and Slot. At least we’re on the podium.”

He added that the Dutch “total football” school was the basis for his own style of football as both a player and a coach.

“To dominate, the game, to take the initiative with the ball, and at the same time our goal is to show to everybody a team with passion, with desire and ambition. That is my philosophy,” he said.

“We are here to compete, we are here to enjoy and we are here to win.”

Senior players

The KNVB’s technical director, Nigel de Jong, said Xavi was identified as a candidate because his footballing philosophy aligned closely with the Dutch team’s ambitions to play “attractive, dominant” football.

The coach said he had not made any decisions about which players he will select, but he had already spoken to current team captain Virgil van Dijk and Barcelona midfielder Frenkie de Jong.

Dutch media have speculated that Van Dijk, 35, and leading scorer Memphis Depay, 32, could be dropped from the squad as part of a clear-out of senior players.

De Jong, who worked with Xavi during the Spaniard’s spell as Barcelona coach from 2021 to 2024, has been struggling with injuries for more than a year and was not fully fit during this year’s World Cup.

The coach also said he had been monitoring AZ Alkmaar’s promising 20-year-old midfielder Kees Smit, who narrowly missed out on the World Cup squad this summer.

Oranje will play their first match under his leadership on September 24, when they take on Germany in the Nations League in Amsterdam. “We haven’t yet decided the [squad] list,” Xavi said. “You will see it in three weeks.”

item.title: Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say
item.description:
Vondelkerk fire investigation ends in mystery, police say

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

How the Vondelkerk in Amsterdam went up in flames on New Year’s Eve is still unknown, police have said, after months of trying and failing to establish a criminal cause for the blaze.

Investigators had looked into whether the fire was started deliberately and whether fireworks were to blame. Local residents were interviewed, video footage examined and tips about possible arson followed up, but none of it produced any evidence, police said.

It could also not be established whether fireworks caused the fire. Much of the forensic evidence was destroyed in the blaze itself, police said, and no traces of fireworks were found. With no leads left to pursue, the investigation has stalled.

Years to rebuild 
The monumental church on Vondelstraat, close to the Vondelpark, was largely destroyed in the early hours of January 1, when its tower collapsed and much of the roof was lost. It was designed by Pierre Cuypers, the 19th-century architect behind Amsterdam’s Centraal station and the Rijksmuseum, and completed in 1880.

The building served as a Catholic church until it closed in 1977 and has since been used for concerts, offices and community events, with church services returning in 2017. It has been owned since 1996 by heritage restoration body Stadsherstel Amsterdam.

Several fundraising drives were launched after the fire. Stadsherstel said more than €180,000 had been raised within a week, and other appeals brought in tens of thousands of euros more. Rebuilding the church is expected to take years.

item.title: Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine
item.description:
Dutch foundation plans to build underground hospital in Ukraine

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A Dutch organisation is trying to raise funds to build a reinforced underground hospital in Ukraine so soldiers can be treated nearer the front line.

Protect Ukraine and a Norwegian foundation, HMM Healthcare, say they have already secured €750,000 in donations for the project, which is expected to cost €2.5 million in total.

The 600 m2 hospital will be built 8 m below ground and made entirely of concrete, allowing wounded service personnel to be treated in what is effectively a giant bunker.

The organisers hope to have the building fully equipped and operational by February 2027.

Jaap Scholten, a Dutch writer and co-founder of Protect Ukraine, said: “The fact that we have raised three-quarters of a million euros in such a short time shows that people in the Netherlands have not forgotten Ukraine.

“But we are not there yet. Every donation brings us closer to a hospital and stabilisation point that can save many lives.”

Protect Ukraine has around 100 volunteers who run regular trips to Ukraine to deliver goods such as medicines, pop-up tents and pick-up trucks.

Scholten, who lives in Hungary, told NOS he started the organisation after watching people in his neighbourhood handing out fresh fruit, energy bars and blankets to Ukrainian refugees.

“Arranging supplies for Ukrainians is the most effective thing you can do to help,” he said. “That’s why I started Protect Ukraine.”

item.title: Many Dutch children hide upsetting online posts from parents
item.description:
Many Dutch children hide upsetting online posts from parents

August 25, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Half of children in the Netherlands aged 10 to 15 sometimes see posts online that frighten or upset them, but many do not tell their parents out of shame or fear of an angry reaction, a government survey has found.

The finding comes as junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts launches a new phase of the government’s Blijf in Beeld (“Stay in the picture”) campaign, which encourages parents to talk to their children about what they encounter online and to agree rules on phone use together.

The survey, commissioned by the economic affairs and climate ministry (EZK), found children in the Netherlands now get their first smartphone at the age of 10 on average. Children most often named Snapchat and TikTok as the places they were most likely to come across something unpleasant.

Talk early
Aerdts said parents should start those conversations while children are young, before the influence of friends grows. “Be curious about what they see, including the nice and funny things,” she said, arguing this makes it easier for children to also raise the frightening or harmful side of social media.

Parents should not judge children for what they do online, she added, and should be open about their own use.

The campaign, developed in part with children’s helpline the Kindertelefoon, comes with a printed card that parents and children fill in together. The ministry said 89.4% of children understood why rules on phone use mattered, and half said they welcomed them.

Waiting for Brussels
Aerdts said platforms were not doing enough to protect children. “The online world is really not yet a safe place for children,” she said, adding that this was why the government wants a minimum age for social media use agreed at European level rather than in national law.

That marks a contrast with France, Spain and Greece, which have moved to set their own age limits. France passed a law last month barring under-15s from social media, though its Constitutional Council then ruled the measure unconstitutional in its current form and the government is redrafting it.

Aerdts has previously said she wants to avoid “a mishmash of rules and regulations that will The European Commission is working on its own proposals: last month researchers advised it to ban social media for children under 13, and commission president Ursula von der Leyen has said she will bring forward a proposal to limit children’s use after the summer.
